initial_observation.demographics: A 43-year-old male with no known past medical history
initial_observation.encounter_context: arrives at the emergency department complaining of fever and headache for the past 5 days
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient denied chest pain, dyspnea, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. The patient was febrile at 38.2°C, tachycardic to 121 beats per minute (bpm), and hypertensive with systolic blood pressure of 168 and diastolic blood pressure of 101 mm Hg. Physical examination including the abdomen was unremarkable. Laboratory assessment showed a white blood cell count of 12,600/mm3 (normal range 4000-11,000/mm3), Aspartate transferase (AST) 48 U/L (normal range <34 U/L), and Alanine transferase (ALT) 83 U/L (normal range 10-49 U/L). An otherwise unremarkable chest X-ray revealed mild elevation of the right hemidiaphragm. The patient was treated with intravenous fluids and acetaminophen with normalization of their vital signs. They were discharged home pending blood culture results.

evidence_items.source_text: The patient was febrile at 38.2°C, tachycardic to 121 beats per minute (bpm), and hypertensive with systolic blood pressure of 168 and diastolic blood pressure of 101 mm Hg.

Laboratory assessment showed a white blood cell count of 12,600/mm3 (normal range 4000-11,000/mm3), Aspartate transferase (AST) 48 U/L (normal range <34 U/L), and Alanine transferase (ALT) 83 U/L (normal range 10-49 U/L).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was performed which revealed a 5.1 × 7.5 × 3.9 cm heterogeneous hypoattenuating lesion in the left hepatic lobe extending up to the lesser curvature of the stomach with and centered over gastro-hepatic recess. There was a rim of peripheral enhancement around the lesion. A hypodense ring paralleling the rim of enhancement was seen around the lesion in the liver often referred to as a double target sign, which is characteristically seen in hepatic abscess. A curvilinear dense foreign body was noted extending from the left hepatic lobe lesion into the gastro-hepatic recess (Figs. 1 and 2). Notably, there was no extraluminal air or significant intraperitoneal fluid that would suggest an active leak from the stomach.

evidence_items.source_text: The abscess grew Streptococcus anginosus and Actinomyces odontolyticus on culture.

During laparoscopy, the greater curvature of the stomach and the anterior surface of the liver appeared grossly normal. There were dense inflammatory adhesions between the anterior gastric wall and the undersurface of the left lobe of the liver, and careful dissection revealed a large amount of purulent fluid which was aspirated and sent for bacterial culture. A moderate amount of fibrinous material adhering the liver surface to the stomach wall was debrided and indicated the abscess had been unroofed. As dissection progressed, an approximately 3 cm white foreign body consistent with a fish bone was removed under direct visualization and sent to pathology (Fig. 3). The stomach was insufflated with air via a nasogastric tube which did not show any obvious leak. The upper abdomen was irrigated, and a drain was placed with the tip in the hepatic abscess cavity and coursing along the anterior wall of the stomach.
Postoperatively, the patient underwent an upper gastrointestinal series which was negative for extravasation of contrast.

After a noneventful postoperative course, the patient was discharged with a drain in place and treated with oral Cefdinir and Metronidazole for 1 week. At the patient's follow-up visit, the patient was recovering well without adverse sequelae from treatment.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: the patient was admitted to the surgical service for the management of a liver abscess, presumed to be secondary to perforation of the stomach by an ingested foreign body
